extraction.name: NWPU-RESISC45
extraction.description: A large-scale, publicly available benchmark dataset for Remote Sensing Image Scene Classification (RESISC), created by Northwestern Polytechnical University (NWPU). It contains 31,500 images, covering 45 scene classes with 700 images in each class. The dataset is large-scale on the number of scene classes and total image number, holds big variations in translation, spatial resolution, viewpoint, object pose, illumination, background, and occlusion, and has high within-class diversity and between-class similarity. The 45 scene classes include land use and land cover classes (e.g., commercial area, farmland, forest, industrial area, mountain, residential area), man-made object classes (e.g., airplane, airport, bridge, church, palace, ship), and landscape nature object classes (e.g., beach, cloud, island, lake, river, sea ice). Images are 256x256 pixels in RGB color space, with spatial resolution varying from about 30m to 0.2m per pixel. The images cover more than 100 countries and regions all over the world, including developing, transition, and highly developed economies.
extraction.creator: Gong Cheng, Junwei Han, Xiaoqiang Lu
extraction.citeAs: Gong Cheng, Junwei Han, and Xiaoqiang Lu, "Remote Sensing Image Scene Classification: Benchmark and State of the Art," Proceedings of the IEEE, 2016.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was constructed by first investigating scene classes from existing datasets to form 30 widely-used categories. Then, 15 additional meaningful scene classes were carefully selected by searching keywords like "OBIA", "GEOBIA", "land cover classification", "land use classification", "geographic image retrieval", and "geospatial object detection" on Web of Science and Google Scholar, resulting in a total of 45 scene classes. Images were carefully selected under various conditions including weathers, seasons, illumination conditions, imaging conditions, and scales to ensure rich variations. Images were obtained to have high within-class diversity and between-class similarity, including fine-grained classes with high semantic overlapping.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Aerial photography and satellite imagery from Google Earth (Google Inc.), which superimposes images obtained from satellite imagery, aerial photography, and geographic information system (GIS) onto a 3D globe.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Images were extracted and classified by experts in the field of remote sensing image interpretation. The classification includes 45 scene classes, encompassing land use and land cover, man-made objects, and landscape nature objects.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Experts in the field of remote sensing image interpretation.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The 31,500 images cover more than 100 countries and regions all over the world, including developing, transition, and highly developed economies, implying geographic information.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset is designed to be challenging by including fine-grained scene classes with high semantic overlapping (e.g., circular farmland and rectangular farmland, commercial area and industrial area, basketball court and tennis court), and possessing high within-class diversity and between-class similarity. This design choice might bias model performance towards methods robust to such complexities.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset's design, featuring high within-class diversity and between-class similarity, and fine-grained scene classes with high semantic overlapping, makes it rather challenging for classification methods and may limit the generalization of simpler models.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Publicly available benchmark for REmote Sensing Image Scene Classification (RESISC). It is intended for developing and evaluating various new data-driven algorithms, especially deep learning-based methods, and for benchmarking state-of-the-art scene classification methods. Specific usage guidelines include splitting the dataset into 10% for training and 90% for testing, or 20% for training and 80% for testing.
